content: Type 1 DM: autoimmune beta-cell destruction, absolute insulin deficiency. Incidence peaks age 5-7 and 10-14 years but can occur at any age. Presentation: polydipsia, polyuria, weight loss, fatigue. Ketosis-prone (risk DKA). C-peptide absent/low. Autoantibodies (anti-GAD, anti-islet cell, anti-IA2) present. Risk: family history (HLA-DR3/DR4), other autoimmune diseases (Hashimoto, celiac, Addison). Lifelong insulin dependence required. Complications: hypoglycemia more frequent than Type 2, retinopathy/nephropathy/neuropathy/CAD common.

topic: Type 2 Diabetes - Pathophysiology and Risk Factors
content: Type 2 DM: insulin resistance + progressive beta-cell dysfunction. Incidence 90-95% of diabetes. Risk: obesity, age >45, family history, physical inactivity, ethnicity (Hispanic, African American, Asian American, Native American). Metabolic syndrome (obesity, hypertension, dyslipidemia) common. Presents insidiously; often asymptomatic at diagnosis (found on screening). C-peptide normal/high initially (preserved secretion). Diagnosis: fasting glucose ≥126, HbA1c ≥6.5%, OGTT ≥200. Non-insulin dependence initially but may require insulin long-term (beta-cell failure).

Gestational DM: glucose intolerance first recognized in pregnancy (not pre-existing). Incidence 2-10% pregnancies. Risk: age, obesity, family history, prior GDM, PCOS. Screening: 50g OGCT at 24-28 weeks; if ≥140, proceed to 3-hour OGTT. Diagnosis: ≥2 abnormal values on OGTT. Management: dietary counseling (carb counting), exercise, insulin often needed (metformin/glyburide safer than other agents in pregnancy). Increases risk gestational HTN, preeclampsia, macrosomia, neonatal hypoglycemia. 50% develop Type 2 DM within 5 years postpartum.

topic: Diabetes Diagnosis - HbA1c, Fasting Glucose, OGTT
content: Diagnostic criteria: fasting glucose ≥126 mg/dL (no calories x8h), random glucose ≥200 with symptoms, HbA1c ≥6.5% (glycosylated hemoglobin, 2-3 month glucose average), 2-hour glucose ≥200 on OGTT (75g glucose load). Prediabetes: fasting 100-125, HbA1c 5.7-6.4%. HbA1c advantages: no fasting required, reflects long-term control. Limitations: hemolytic anemia (false low), hemoglobin variants affect accuracy. Values repeat for confirmation (except symptomatic hyperglycemia). Self-monitoring: home glucose logs, continuous glucose monitors (CGM).

HbA1c targets individualized: <7% for non-fragile adults (lower risk, good functional status). <8% for fragile elderly, limited life expectancy, hypoglycemia-prone. <6.5% controversial in Type 2 (increased mortality in some trials, intensive therapy-related). Very high targets (8-9%) acceptable if severe hypoglycemia, limited access, advanced complications. Factors: age, comorbidities, hypoglycemia awareness, medication burden, renal/liver disease. Adjust targets at 3-6 month intervals based on HbA1c, patient tolerance, hypoglycemia frequency. Patient preference critical; shared decision-making preferred over rigid targets.

Metformin (biguanide): first-line agent for Type 2 DM. Mechanism: decreases hepatic glucose production (gluconeogenesis), improves insulin sensitivity. Benefits: weight-neutral, no hypoglycemia, cardiovascular benefit, rhabdomyolysis rare. Dosing: 500-2000 mg daily (BID-TID, extended-release available). Contraindication: GFR <30 (risk lactic acidosis from accumulation); caution if GFR 30-45. Side effects: GI (nausea, diarrhea, 30% patients), vitamin B12 deficiency (monitor annually), lactic acidosis (very rare if renal function normal). Iodinated contrast: hold metformin 48h after contrast (risk acute renal injury + lactic acidosis), restart if renal function stable.

Sulfonylureas (glyburide, glipizide, glimepiride): increase insulin secretion. Mechanism: block ATP-sensitive K+ channels on beta cells, increase insulin release. Benefits: effective glucose lowering (HbA1c -1-2%), inexpensive, oral. Risk: hypoglycemia (15-20% vs 5% with metformin), weight gain, secondary failure (beta-cell exhaustion). Meglitinides (repaglinide, nateglinide): similar mechanism, shorter-acting, pre-meal dosing. Lower hypoglycemia risk than sulfonylureas but still present. Both contraindicated if recurrent hypoglycemia, hypoglycemia unawareness, renal/hepatic disease. Preference shifted to newer agents (SGLT2i, GLP-1) with cardiovascular/renal benefits.

topic: SGLT2 Inhibitors - Cardiovascular and Renal Benefits
content: SGLT2 inhibitors (empagliflozin, canagliflozin, dapagliflozin): block renal glucose reabsorption, increase urinary glucose excretion. Benefits: HbA1c -0.5-1%, weight loss, blood pressure reduction, cardiovascular mortality reduction (EMPA-REG OUTCOME, CANVAS), heart failure benefit, CKD slowing. Side effects: genital mycotic infection (10%), diabetic ketoacidosis (euglycemic DKA if SGLT2i), dehydration (diuretic effect), amputation risk (canagliflozin, less with other agents). Contraindication: DKA (or euglycemic DKA risk), type 1 DM (euglycemic DKA risk), severe renal disease (GFR <20). Monitor volume status, renal function. Advantageous in CKD, heart failure, obesity.

topic: GLP-1 Receptor Agonists - Weight Loss and CV Protection
content: GLP-1 agonists (liraglutide, dulaglutide, semaglutide, tirzepatide): incretin mimetics, increase insulin secretion (glucose-dependent), slow gastric emptying, reduce appetite. Benefits: HbA1c -1-1.8%, weight loss 2-5 kg, cardiovascular mortality reduction, GFR stabilization. Side effects: nausea, vomiting, diarrhea (40%), pancreatitis risk (controversial), thyroid C-cell tumors (animal studies; unknown human risk). Contraindication: personal/family history medullary thyroid cancer, MEN-2 syndrome, acute pancreatitis. Injection weekly (some agents). Cost barrier in some regions. Superior to other agents in weight loss, CV benefit.

DPP-4 inhibitors (sitagliptin, linagliptin): enhance endogenous GLP-1 by blocking dipeptidyl peptidase-4. Benefits: modest glucose lowering (HbA1c -0.5-0.8%), weight-neutral, no hypoglycemia, oral daily dosing, well-tolerated. Drawbacks: less effective than metformin or GLP-1, no CV/renal benefit clear. Useful in renal disease (linagliptin preferred). Thiazolidinediones (pioglitazone, rosiglitazone): insulin sensitizers, increase adipose glucose uptake. Benefits: HbA1c -1-1.5%, CV benefit (pioglitazone in high-risk Type 2). Drawbacks: weight gain, fluid retention (HF risk), bone loss, bladder cancer risk (pioglitazone, controlled). Rarely first-line now; reserved for specific indications.

topic: Insulin Types and Regimens - Basal-Bolus Strategy
content: Insulin types: rapid-acting (aspart, lispro, glulisine, 5-15 min onset), short-acting (regular, 30-60 min), intermediate (NPH, 2-4 hours), long-acting (glargine U100, degludec U200, 24 hours). Regimens: basal-bolus (long-acting basal daily + rapid-acting with meals) preferred for Type 1; sliding scale (rapid-acting per glucose readings) less preferred (reactive not proactive). Dosing: 0.5-1 unit/kg daily split basal/bolus (50% each); adjust by 2-4 units every 3 days per glucose logs/HbA1c. Premix insulin (70/30 NPH/regular, 75/25 lispro/protamine): convenient x2 daily but less flexible. Insulin pump (continuous SC infusion) for Type 1, selected Type 2.

Hypoglycemia: glucose <70 mg/dL. Symptoms: tremor, diaphoresis, palpitations, anxiety, hunger (adrenergic), confusion, slurred speech, seizure (neuroglycopenic). Symptomatic <70 treated immediately. Rule of 15: 15g carbohydrate (4 oz juice, 3-4 dextrose tablets, 1 tbsp honey), recheck at 15 minutes, repeat if still <100. Follow with long-acting carbohydrate (bread, milk). Severe hypoglycemia (seizure, LOC): glucagon 1mg IM/IV, then carbohydrates when able. Prevention: patient education, frequent monitoring (CGM), realistic targets, medication adjustment. Hypoglycemia unawareness (loss of adrenergic warning): risk with long-standing diabetes, tight control, autonomic neuropathy; requires relaxed targets.

DKA (diabetic ketoacidosis): acute life-threatening condition with: pH <7.3, HCO3- <15, elevated ketones (beta-hydroxybutyrate >3), anion gap metabolic acidosis. Pathophysiology: insulin deficiency leads to hyperglycemia, osmotic diuresis, dehydration; free fatty acid mobilization leads to ketone production. Usually Type 1 but can occur Type 2. Triggers: infection (50%), non-adherence, new-onset diabetes, medications (steroids, SGLT2i). Presentation: polydipsia, polyuria, Kussmaul respirations (deep rapid breathing, fruity breath from acetone), nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, altered mental status (more severe hyperglycemia/hyperosmolality). Mortality 1-5% if treated, >15% if delayed.

topic: DKA Treatment - Fluids, Insulin, Electrolyte Repletion
content: DKA treatment: (1) IV fluids: 0.9% NS 500-1000 mL/hr initially (aggressive hydration), switch to 0.45% NS once glucose <250. Total deficit typically 5-10L. (2) Insulin: bolus 0.1 units/kg IV, then 0.1 units/kg/hr continuous infusion (usually 5-10 units/hr), titrate to reduce glucose 50-75 mg/dL/hr. (3) Potassium: check baseline; likely total body deficit 3-5 mEq/kg despite normal/high serum K+ (shifts). Replete cautiously (K+ shift into cells with insulin = hypokalemia risk). (4) Bicarbonate: controversial, reserved for pH <6.9 (3 amps NaHCO3 in D5W). Monitor: glucose, electrolytes, ABG q1-2h initially, neuro checks. Switch to SC insulin once ketosis resolves (glucose <200, HCO3- >15, eating).

HHS (hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state): acute hyperglycemic emergency, usually Type 2 (older, renal/cardiac comorbidities). Diagnostic: glucose >600 mg/dL, osmolality >320 (calculated = 2[Na] + glucose/18 + BUN/2.8), minimal/absent ketonemia (pH usually >7.30, HCO3- >15), often altered mental status. Triggers: infection, medication non-adherence, medications (steroids, antipsychotics). More common in older patients, higher mortality (15-20% even treated) than DKA. Pathophysiology: residual insulin prevents ketosis but cannot lower glucose; severe hyperglycemia causes osmotic diuresis, severe dehydration. Treatment similar to DKA but slower glucose reduction (25-50 mg/dL/hr risk osmotic edema/stroke), more aggressive fluid repletion, insulin lower-dose.

topic: Sick Day Management and Glycemic Control in Hospital
content: Sick day management: increase glucose monitoring (q2-4h), stay hydrated, take medications as usual (especially insulin; never stop). Hyperglycemia response: if glucose >250, check for DKA/HHS signs. Hypoglycemia: treat per protocol. Nausea/vomiting: small frequent meals/liquids, antiemetics, IV fluids if severe. Hospital glycemic control: target 140-180 mg/dL (lower targets increase hypoglycemia risk). Insulin-only regimens (hold other agents): basal-bolus IV insulin (0.5 units/kg/24h basal, additional bolus per carb intake). Subcutaneous insulin resumption when: eating, hemodynamically stable, not in DKA/HHS. Avoid hypoglycemia <70 (impairs recovery, increases infection risk, cardiovascular events).

Retinopathy: nonproliferative (microaneurysms, dot-blot hemorrhages) to proliferative (neovascularization, vitreous hemorrhage, retinal detachment). Screening: annual dilated eye exam. Treatment: tight glucose/BP control, laser photocoagulation, anti-VEGF injections. Nephropathy: early albuminuria, progressing to chronic kidney disease, end-stage renal disease. Screening: urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio, eGFR. Prevention: tight glucose control, ACE-I/ARB (renal protection), SGLT2i. Neuropathy: distal sensory polyneuropathy (loss protective sensation, ulcer risk), autonomic (orthostatic HTN, erectile dysfunction, gastroparesis). Management: glucose control, gabapentin, pregabalin for pain. Screening: annual monofilament testing, vibration sense, ankle reflexes.

CAD: diabetes increases risk 2-4 fold, multiple infarcts possible, silent ischemia common. Screening: EKG baseline, stress testing if high risk, CAC score controversial. Treatment: aggressive lipid/BP control, dual antiplatelet therapy post-event, revascularization if indicated. Stroke: atherosclerotic and cardioembolic mechanisms. Increased risk with diabetes + HTN + dyslipidemia. Prevention: aspirin, tight BP/lipid/glucose control, carotid imaging if symptomatic. Peripheral artery disease (PAD): claudication, critical limb ischemia, amputation risk. Treatment: walking program, cilostazol, revascularization, foot care (prevent ulcers). Aggressive risk factor modification decreases CV events 20-50%.
